subtopic: Sparse vs dense kernel boundary / When sparsity pays
learningObjective: Identify when unstructured or structured sparsity actually reduces wall-clock time on GPU, vs when it only reduces FLOP count.

hardwareContext.architecture: Ampere or newer for 2:4 sparse tensor cores

stem: Select all statements that correctly characterize the boundary between sparse and dense GPU kernels. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Unstructured sparsity (arbitrary zero pattern) rarely translates to wall-clock speedup on GPU unless density is well below ~10%, because indexing overhead and irregular memory access outweigh the FLOP reduction on tensor-core-driven dense hardware.

Structured 2:4 sparsity (Ampere) preserves tensor-core throughput at half the FLOP cost of the equivalent dense GEMM; it is a hardware-native format supported by cuSPARSELt / cuBLAS sparse APIs and yields real speedup on supported dtypes.

For LLM inference, weight sparsity that reduces HBM traffic (e.g., N:M or block-sparse weight formats) is more impactful than FLOP reduction, because decode is bandwidth-bound. However, this only works if a compatible sparse kernel exists for the target dtype.

Any percentage of sparsity greater than 50% in a weight matrix automatically gives a proportional wall-clock speedup on modern GPUs, since sparse tensor-cores dynamically skip zero tiles regardless of the sparsity pattern.

explanation: A is correct: unstructured sparsity on GPUs typically needs very low density before its FLOP savings beat the overhead of irregular indexing and load-imbalance across warps. C is correct: LLM decode is bandwidth-bound on weight/KV reads, so any sparse format that reduces bytes read is directly beneficial — provided a matching sparse kernel exists. B is partially correct as a factual statement about 2:4 but oversells 'yields real speedup' without conditions; the phrasing here treats it as an unconditional claim, which we do not accept as strictly correct — this option is meant as a distractor about how narrowly the 2:4 support is: it is only for specific dtypes (FP16/BF16/INT8) and requires dedicated kernels. D is wrong: 'sparse tensor cores dynamically skip zero tiles regardless of pattern' is fabricated; hardware requires the 2:4 structure.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: unstructured sparsity break-even point on GPU is very low density.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: decode is bandwidth-bound; sparsity that reduces HBM traffic can help if a kernel exists.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong (as stated): 2:4 does provide speedup but only on supported dtypes and with dedicated kernels; the option's blanket 'yields real speedup' is unconditional and misleading.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: hardware requires the 2:4 structure; arbitrary sparsity does not get hardware-native skipping.

assumptions: GPU refers to modern NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere and newer).
'Sparse kernel' means a specialized kernel that reads only nonzeros and their indices.
nonImplications: Does not imply that sparsity never helps; it does at extreme sparsity or with structured formats.
Does not imply block-sparse and 2:4 are equivalent; they trade regularity for compression differently.

performanceClaim.scope: Sparse vs dense wall-clock speedup on GPU
